2.1.5 Geologic Hazards
The project is located in zone 2 of the seismic risk map of the United States where moderate damage to structures from earthquake has occurred; however, the geologic hazard as related to the regional seismicity is considered negligible due to the foundation and dam design. The residual soil foundation at Bad Creek is not susceptible to liquefaction and the dam design is such that potential damage from earthquake is very small.
2.2 SPECIES AND ECOSYSTEMS
2.2.1 Flora
Dr. Leland Rodgers of Furman University, South Carolina, conducted a survey of the vascular flora of the project area. His findings are included in Appendix D of Applicant's Exhibit W and in a pamphlet by Dr. Rodgers entitled, "Flowers, Ferns, Shrubs, and Trees found at Keowee-Toxaway." Other sources containing information on vascular species in this area are Radford, et al. (1968), Cooper (1963), and Fernald (1970).
The vegetation of the area is primarily second growth forest (Figure 2-1), which has been logged, in many cases several times, and is presently managed for timber production. There are many escarpment gorges in and adjacent to the project area. A general description of the vegetation can be ascertained from vegetation studies of specific gorges (Toxaway Gorge: Cooper, 1963; Horsepasture Gorge: Rodgers, 1965; Bearcamp Creek Watershed: Rodgers and Shake, 1965; and Thompson Gorge: Racine, 1969). Five broad vegetation units (Table 2-2) are commonly found in escarpment gorges (Cooper and Hardin, 1971). These are discussed below in the order they are distributed from the riverside to higher elevations.
